findings.description: No server_side_encryption_configuration is set, so objects in this bucket are stored unencrypted at rest, and no ACL/public access block is defined leaving default access ambiguous.
The bucket lacks any aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block or explicit private ACL, so it may be reachable publicly depending on account defaults, exposing archived reports.
No server_side_encryption_configuration block is specified, so sensitive ledger export data is stored without encryption at rest.
No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined for this bucket, leaving model artifacts unencrypted at rest.
No server_side_encryption_configuration is defined, so operational runbook content (which may contain credentials or internal procedures) is unencrypted at rest.

The acl value "lcatalogopts-delivery-write" is not a standard S3 canned ACL; if this is intended to be 'log-delivery-write' it grants broad write access to the logging service, and if misconfigured/invalid it may fail closed or open in unexpected ways. Canned ACLs like log-delivery-write allow other AWS accounts to write to the bucket, which combined with force_destroy and audit data sensitivity increases risk of tampering with audit logs.

The object is uploaded without specifying server-side encryption (kms_key_id or server_side_encryption), and it is placed into a bucket that itself has no default encryption, so the vendor roster file (potentially sensitive) is stored unencrypted.

force_destroy = true allows the bucket and all its contents to be deleted in a single terraform destroy/apply operation without object protection, increasing risk of irreversible data loss if access controls or automation are compromised.
